newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks to boost aid to Jordan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks to boost aid to Jordan.

text.p: The United States said on Thursday it was seeking ways to give Jordan more aid and did not rule out taking the money from its traditional allocation to Israel, the largest U.S. aid recipient at about $3 billion a year.
"There are a number of options being debated within our government and being discussed with countries, including Israel," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

"I don't want to go into those publicly. But I do want to put the accent mark ... on the following -- Jordan deserves our support because of King Hussein's leadership. And we are actively trying to find ways to get that support."

Generally, aid for Israel and, to a lesser extent Egypt, has been considered sacrosanct, even though the U.S. foreign aid budget has decreased significantly in recent years with many countries seeing their allocations cut or ended.
African countries have been particularly hard hit.

Asked if aid to Israel remained sacrosanct, Burns said: "...there are a number of options being considered ... the adminstration hasn't made a decision ... we haven't had an opportunity to have full discussions with the U.S. Congress, which holds the purse strings."

Although he said Israel and Egypt would certainly continue to receive U.S. aid, he would not commit to the level of that assistance, saying "that's a decision the Congress and the adminstration will have to make together."
Israel Radio reported earlier on Thursday that U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, on a trip to the region, raised the issue of a possible $50 million cut in U.S. aid in talks with Israeli officials.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy is due in Washington on Friday for talks with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. Burns said he did not know if the aid issue would come up.

Egypt receives about $2 billion annually. The huge assistance programmes derive from the U.S. committment to support the two countries in their peace efforts. They signed a treaty, the first between Israel and its Arab enemies, in 1979.
Jordan received $47 million in U.S. economic and military aid in 1997 and President Clinton asked for $75.6 million in his 1998 budget request.

Burns said the administration was "doing all we can to assist all the countries in the Middle East that support the peace negotiations" and for some time has been seeking ways to provide "substantial" economic assistance to Jordan.

"King Hussein has taken a genuine risk for peace and he deserves the support of the United States. He has been a courageous leader and a visionary leader -- particularly during the last six months or so -- in the search for peace," the spokesman said.

Peace negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians are stalemated, as are talks between Israel and Syria. Burns said talk of boosting aid to Jordan was not meant to underscore American frustration with Israel in the search for peace.
Israel was upbeat on Thursday but the PLO said Ross failed to make progress despite convening a high-level meeting Wednesday of Israeli and Palestinains officials on restarting formal peace talks.
Burns reinforced Ross's assessment that the meeting was useful. "It is important to have meetings," he said.
Congress, with a large contingent of pro-Israel members, has traditionally resisted any effort to reduce aid to the Jewish state. That resistance is expected to continue.

This year the administration is seeking its first increase in the overall foreign aid budget in quite some time. The request totals $19.5 billion, up 7 percent from 1997, including a large rise in aid to the former Soviet Union.
